property_summary: Invariant: Only the Owner can cause the contract balance to be drained by withdraw() — after any call to withdraw(), if the caller was not the Owner then the contract balance remains unchanged; the mutant removing the require allows a non-Owner caller to drain the balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For all callers and amounts, if a non-owner calls withdraw the contract balance remains with the contract (i.e., withdraw only succeeds in transferring the full balance when called by Owner); the mutant removing the require allows a non-owner to drain the balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every caller and any contract balance, only the Owner can successfully withdraw the contract's ether (calls to withdraw revert for non-owners); the mutant removes the require so some non-owner caller can successfully withdraw and thus violates this rule.

For all callers and any nonzero contract balance, only the Owner can cause the contract to transfer out the balance via withdraw() (i.e., when a non-owner calls withdraw, the contract's balance remains unchanged); the mutant removing the require lets a non-owner drain the contract, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every caller and any initial contract balance > 0, when withdraw() is invoked by the caller the reference preserves that the contract's balance becomes zero only if the caller is the Owner (i.e., non-owners do not receive the funds); the mutant removing the require allows some non-owner caller to cause the contract balance to drop to zero.

For any caller who is the Owner and any contract balance, calling withdraw() always sends the entire contract balance to the stored Owner address (so address(c).balance == 0 after the call and Owner's balance increases); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can send the funds to a different address and thus break the property (address(c).balance != 0 or Owner did not receive the funds) for some inputs.

For any caller who is the stored Owner and for any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw() always empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0) in the reference; the mutant that transfers to msg.sender can leave the contract non-empty or divert funds, so there exists an input (an owner caller with some balance) that makes address(c).balance != 0 after withdraw on the mutant.

For any caller who is the stored Owner and for any contract balance, after Owner calls withdraw() the contract balance becomes zero (the Owner always receives the funds); the mutant that pays msg.sender instead can divert funds away from Owner causing the property to fail for some inputs.

For any caller that is the stored Owner and for any initial nonzero contract balance, after Owner calls withdraw() the Owner address's balance increases by exactly the pre-call contract balance (i.e., Owner receives the contract funds); the mutant sending funds to msg.sender can cause Owner's balance to NOT increase by that amount for some inputs.

For any caller who is the stored Owner and any contract balance, when Owner calls withdraw() the contract's balance becomes zero (the Owner receives the contract funds); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender can leave the contract nonzero for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For any caller who is the Owner and any contract balance, calling withdraw() sends the entire contract balance to Owner (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers only half breaks this by leaving a nonzero balance for some inputs.

For any caller who is Owner and any nonzero contract balance funded by that Owner, calling withdraw() empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers only half violates this by leaving a nonzero balance for some fuzzed funding amounts.

For any caller equal to Owner and any initial nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw() forwards the entire contract balance to Owner leaving address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that transfers only half will leave a nonzero balance for some fuzzed funding amounts and thus violate this rule.

For any caller equal to Owner, after Owner calls withdraw() the contract balance becomes strictly less than or equal to its previous balance and in the reference it becomes zero (i.e. withdraw fully empties the contract), whereas the mutant that transfers only half can leave a strictly positive balance for some funded amounts; we assert address(c).balance == 0 after Owner calls withdraw().

For any Owner caller and any nonzero contract balance funded by any address, after Owner calls withdraw() the reference transfers the entire contract balance away (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers only half can leave a positive balance, so the property asserts address(c).balance == 0 after Owner withdraws.

For any caller and any balance, calling withdraw from the contract succeeds (does not revert) and transfers out the contract balance when msg.sender == Owner; the mutant that adds require(msg.sender != Owner) makes withdraw revert when the Owner calls it, so there exists an input (Owner calling) that breaks this property.

For every caller address and amount, when the contract Owner calls withdraw it succeeds (does not revert) and leaves address(c).balance == 0; the mutant adding require(msg.sender != Owner) makes Owner calls revert, violating this rule for some input (Owner as caller).

For any caller address and any value, when the contract Owner calls withdraw it succeeds (does not revert) and empties the contract balance; the mutant that adds `require(msg.sender != Owner)` causes Owner calls to revert and thus breaks this rule for some input (Owner as caller).

For any caller address and any deposit amount, if a call to withdraw is invoked by the contract Owner then the call succeeds (does not revert); the mutant that adds require(msg.sender != Owner) causes Owner invocations to revert, violating this rule for some input.

For every address caller and any deposit amount, if the contract Owner calls withdraw then the call succeeds (does not revert); the mutant that adds require(msg.sender != Owner) makes Owner calls revert, so the property is violated for inputs where the fuzzer chooses the Owner as the caller and a nonzero balance is present.

For any caller and any payable amount, when Command is invoked by Owner forwarding msg.value, the contract's balance after the call equals its prior balance plus msg.value (i.e., Command forwards ETH into the call causing no loss from c); the mutant that drops value forwarding can change c.balance for some calldata/recipient behavior and thus violates this invariant.

For any caller-supplied amount and target, when Owner calls Command forwarding ETH, the reference C always ends with the same contract balance as before the call (it forwards the ETH to the callee so balance does not decrease), whereas the mutant that drops msg.value can cause the contract balance to increase (because the callee receives no value) — so we assert that after Owner calls Command forwarding value to a malicious reverter callee, address(c).balance remains equal to the pre-call balance for the reference but the mutant will sometimes violate this.

For any owner-supplied ETH value and any calldata, when the Owner calls Command forwarding msg.value to an arbitrary callee contract whose fallback/receive accepts ETH and records how much it received, the reference C always forwards the same msg.value so address(c).balance decreases by exactly msg.value (i.e., the callee receives those funds and c's balance is reduced by msg.value), while the mutant that drops value forwarding can leave c's balance unchanged (or decrease by a different amount) for some inputs — so the invariant is: after Owner calls Command forwarding value V to a callee that accepts ETH, address(c).balance == priorBalance - V; the mutant can violate this for some fuzzed V and callee code.

For any owner-invoked Command forwarding some ETH to a callee that reverts on receiving value, the reference contract always ends with c.balance unchanged (the ETH is forwarded and reverted so refunded to c), whereas the mutant that drops msg.value can cause c.balance to increase or remain different because no ETH was forwarded—so address(c).balance after the call always equals the prior balance for the reference, but the mutant can violate it for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any calldata and value, when Owner calls Command forwarding ETH to a callee that records whether it received any ETH (via payable fallback/receive), the reference always forwards the msg.value so the callee's recorded receivedAmount equals the sent msg.value (and c's balance decreases by that same msg.value); the mutant that drops forwarding can produce a call where the callee records receivedAmount == 0 while msg.value > 0, violating this.

For any caller and any calldata/ETH sent, when the Owner calls Command the contract balance after the call equals the balance before the call plus the msg.value (i.e., Command never empties the contract balance); the mutant violates this by transferring the entire contract balance to Owner before executing the call, making post-call balance smaller for some inputs.

For any caller and any calldata/value, when Owner calls Command the contract balance after Command equals the pre-call balance plus msg.value (i.e., Command does not withdraw existing balance); the mutant breaks this by transferring the existing contract balance to Owner before executing the call causing post-call contract balance to be less than pre+msg.value for some inputs.

For any caller and any sent value, when multiplicate is called the correct contract always drains its entire resulting balance (address(c).balance becomes 0 after the call); the mutant that omits adding msg.value can leave a non-zero balance for some inputs (fuzzer will find such inputs).

For any caller and any msg.value where msg.value >= address(c).balance at call time, the reference contract sends the entire post-call funds out so address(c).balance == 0 afterwards; the mutant that omits adding msg.value can leave a non-zero contract balance for some such inputs.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) with msg.value >= address(c).balance where adr is a contract whose fallback accepts Ether, the reference C forwards at least msg.value + preBalance (draining the contract) so address(c).balance == 0 afterwards; the mutant that omits adding msg.value can leave a non-zero balance for some admissible inputs.

For any caller address A and any msg.value >= contract balance, when multiplicate(A) is called and the recipient's fallback REVERTS, the reference contract will still transfer the contract's entire post-call balance (causing the call to multiplicate to revert due to transfer reverting), whereas the mutant sending only pre-balance may not revert in the same situations; thus the reference always causes multiplicate to revert (ok==false) for some combinations where mutant succeeds (ok==true).

For any caller and any msg.value, when multiplicate is invoked with msg.value >= preBalance and the recipient is a contract whose fallback REFUSES to accept the extra incoming msg.value (i.e., reverts when receiving more than the contract's current balance), the reference C will attempt to transfer the full post-call balance (preBalance + msg.value) causing the call to revert; the mutant that omits msg.value from the transfer will sometimes succeed — hence the property: when calling multiplicate on a recipient that reverts on receiving >preBalance, the reference always reverts (ok == false) while the mutant can return ok == true for some fuzzed inputs.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) with any msg.value, the reference contract transfers the entire post-call balance to adr whenever msg.value >= prior balance (so the call succeeds and drains the contract); the mutant requiring msg.value > prior balance fails to transfer when msg.value == prior balance, so there exists inputs (msg.value equal to prior balance) that make the mutant behave differently.

For every call to multiplicate(adr), if msg.value is at least the contract's prior balance then the reference C will transfer the full post-call balance to adr; the mutant requiring msg.value > prior balance fails to transfer when msg.value == prior balance, so there exists inputs (msg.value == prior balance) that make the mutant behave differently.

For every call to multiplicate(adr), if msg.value is at least the contract's prior balance then the reference transfers the contract's entire post-call balance away (so address(c).balance becomes 0), while the mutant requiring msg.value > prior balance fails to transfer when msg.value == prior balance, leaving a nonzero contract balance — the test fuzzes a sender and an amount to expose msg.value == prior balance behavior.

For all inputs where the caller sends msg.value equal to the contract's prior balance, the reference C will transfer the entire post-call balance away (leaving address(c).balance == 0) but the mutant requiring msg.value > balance will not — so the invariant is that when msg.value == priorBalance, after multiplicate the reference leaves address(c).balance == 0.

For any caller and any amount, if multiplicate is invoked with msg.value >= prior contract balance then the reference contract always transfers the entire post-call balance away (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that changes >= to > is violated for the specific case msg.value == priorBalance because it will not transfer, leaving a nonzero balance.

For any call to multiplicate(adr) funded with value >= contract balance, the reference C always forwards the entire contract balance+msg.value to the target (so address(c).balance becomes 0 and the call completes), whereas the mutant inverts the condition and will not forward when msg.value>=balance (causing address(c).balance to remain nonzero for some fuzzed inputs).

For any caller and amount where the caller sends at least the current contract balance, calling multiplicate(target) always empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0) in the reference; the mutant inverts the branch and can leave nonzero balance for some such inputs.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) where msg.sender is the contract Owner and msg.value >= address(c).balance, the reference C always empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0) after the call; the mutant inverts the branch and can leave a nonzero balance for some such inputs.

For any caller and value where msg.sender is the Owner and msg.value < address(c).balance, the reference C never transfers funds (leaving address(c).balance unchanged); the mutant inverts the branch and will transfer in that case, changing address(c).balance.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) by any sender with any msg.value, the reference contract never increases its own balance (it either stays the same or becomes zero because it forwards funds), whereas the mutant's inverted condition can cause the contract to retain funds it would have forwarded — observable as address(c).balance being nonzero when reference guarantees it would be zero for certain inputs.

For every call to multiplicate(adr) with some msg.value, the reference contract never transfers more Ether than the contract's balance plus msg.value only when that sum would overflow the checked condition (the require prevents an unintended large transfer); the mutant omits the require and can cause the transfer to succeed in cases where the checked inequality would have prevented it (observable as address(c).balance becoming zero when it shouldn't or causing an unexpected successful transfer).

For any caller and any value, when multiplicate(...) is invoked with msg.value strictly greater-or-equal to the contract balance, the reference C will only transfer the sum (address(this).balance + msg.value) if that sum is >= the previous balance (i.e., no wraparound); the mutant removing the require can cause the transfer to occur when the arithmetic would have wrapped (or violate the inequality), leading to an unexpected successful transfer — we detect this by observing address(c).balance going to zero only when the reference would prevent it.

For all callers and amounts, the reference contract never allows multiplicate to succeed in emptying the contract balance (transfer out balance+msg.value) when msg.value>=address(this).balance but the checked require would fail (i.e., when (address(this).balance + msg.value) < address(this).balance due to wrap/overflow conditions); the mutant removes that require and can thus make multiplicate succeed in cases where the reference would prevent the transfer.

For every admissible caller and ether amount, calling multiplicate(adr) never succeeds in transferring out the contract's funds when the post-addition sum would be strictly less than the previous contract balance (i.e., (address(this).balance + msg.value) < previous_balance) — the reference enforces this via require and thus either prevents the transfer (call reverts) or leaves address(c).balance unchanged; the mutant removes the require and can succeed for some inputs, draining funds, so the property is violated for some fuzzed inputs.
